nameStory: The Least Sandpiper earns its name by being the smallest shorebird in the world – a tiny dynamo among its larger cousins. The scientific name Calidris minutilla literally means "very small" in Medieval Latin, emphasizing just how petite these birds really are. Ancient Greeks used the term "kalidris" for grey-colored waterside birds, showing that people have been watching these busy little shorebirds for thousands of years.
description: The Least Sandpiper is a sparrow-sized shorebird that's perfectly built for life on mudflats and marsh edges. These compact little birds have brownish streaked plumage that looks like they've been dusted with sand and earth tones. They're constantly in motion, running along shorelines on tiny legs, probing the mud with their thin, pointed bills. Despite being the world's smallest sandpiper, they're mighty travelers that can migrate thousands of miles between their Arctic breeding grounds and wintering areas.

idTips.label: Yellow-green legs
idTips.description: Look for distinctive yellowish or greenish-yellow legs that stand out against dark mud – they look almost lime-colored in good light and are noticeably different from the black legs of similar sandpipers

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: About the size of a large sparrow, noticeably smaller than other sandpipers – they look almost toy-like when mixed in with larger shorebirds

idTips.label: Brown streaked plumage
idTips.description: Rich brown and buff coloring with darker streaks, like coffee with cream – much browner and warmer-toned than the grayer Semipalmated Sandpiper

idTips.label: Thin, pointed bill
idTips.description: Fine, needle-like bill that's straight and dark, perfect for picking tiny invertebrates from soft mud – feels delicate if you handle a bird during banding

idTips.label: Hunched feeding posture
idTips.description: Often feeds with a distinctive crouched, almost mouse-like posture as they pick at the surface rather than probing deeply

idTips.label: High-pitched peep call
idTips.description: Makes a thin, rising "kreep" or "preep" sound that's higher and thinner than other sandpipers – sounds almost like a tiny squeeze toy

habitat: Least Sandpipers prefer muddy edges of salt marshes, tidal pools, and mudflats where their tiny legs can navigate soft substrates. They're often found along the quieter, more sheltered areas of coastal estuaries rather than open ocean beaches, and will also visit freshwater pond edges and marshy areas inland. Look for them in spots where the mud is rich with tiny invertebrates and where they can easily wade in shallow water.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration brings flocks through New England in May, when birds show their brightest breeding plumage with rich brown and buff tones. They're often mixed with other sandpiper species at prime mudflat locations.
seasonality.summer: Most birds continue north to Arctic breeding grounds, but some non-breeding individuals may linger at coastal sites. Any Least Sandpipers present are usually in worn, faded plumage.
seasonality.fall: Migration peaks again from July through September, with birds showing fresher fall plumage. Juveniles with crisp, scaly-looking back feathers often appear alongside adults.
seasonality.winter: Some individuals winter along the southern New England coast, particularly in protected salt marsh areas where they can find unfrozen feeding spots during mild periods.

funFact: Despite weighing less than a slice of bread (about 20 grams), Least Sandpipers can fly nonstop for over 2,000 miles during migration – that's like a person running from Boston to Denver without stopping to eat or rest!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Semipalmated Sandpiper, but remember "yellow shoes" for Least versus "black boots" for Semipalmated. Least Sandpipers also have a browner, warmer appearance while Semipalmated look grayer and cooler-toned, and Least have a more hunched feeding posture.
contextualKnowledge: The name "sandpiper" can be misleading since many species, including the Least, actually prefer muddy areas over sandy beaches. The "peep" is a common nickname used by birders for the smallest, hardest-to-identify sandpipers, and Least Sandpipers are the classic example of this challenging group.
compareHints: Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling. It's also much browner than the gray-and-white Sanderling and lacks the Dunlin's longer, curved bill. While White-rumped Sandpiper is similar in size, it shows a distinctive white rump patch in flight that Least Sandpipers lack.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
